title: Is the Number of One-Bits Even or Odd?

concept.title: XOR the halves of the number onto each other until one bit holds the parity
body: The *parity* of a number's binary representation is whether the **number of 1-bits is even or odd**. For `3 = 11` it is even (2 ones), for `7 = 111` it is odd (3 ones). Parity bits are used to detect single-bit errors in data transmission. For each question number print `even` or `odd`.

You could count the ones and look at the remainder modulo 2. A cleverer way uses XOR, because `1 ^ 1 = 0`: **XOR of a group of bits is 1 exactly when the group has an odd number of ones**. So the parity of a 64-bit number is the XOR of all its 64 bits. XOR the upper half onto the lower half: `x ^= x >> 32` — now the low 32 bits hold the XOR of the pairs, and the parity of the whole number is the parity of the low 32 bits. Repeat with 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. After the last step the lowest bit is the parity.

body.code:
for x in numbers:
    x ^= x >> 32
    x ^= x >> 16
    x ^= x >> 8
    x ^= x >> 4
    x ^= x >> 2
    x ^= x >> 1
    answer.append("odd" if x & 1 else "even")      # the lowest bit is the parity
print(*answer)

body: Each folding halves the number of bits that matter, so six steps handle 64 bits, a fixed amount of work for every number (no loop over the ones). This "fold by halves" idea also computes the popcount and reverses bits in parallel inside one machine word.

statement: For each of the `q` given numbers print `odd` if its binary representation has an odd number of 1-bits, and `even` otherwise.
inputFormat: The first line has `q`: the number of questions.
outputFormat: Print `q` words (`even` or `odd`) on one line, separated by spaces.

examples.note: 1 and 8 have one 1-bit, 7 has three (odd); 3 has two (even): odd even odd odd.

hints: XOR of all the bits of the number is its parity.
Fold the number onto itself: x ^= x >> 32, then 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
The lowest bit then holds the answer.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

q = int(input())
ns = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: The upper half of the 64 bits is XORed onto the lower half (shift by 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1); after the last step the lowest bit is the XOR of all the bits, which is 1 exactly when the number of 1-bits is odd.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

q = int(input())
ns = list(map(int, input().split()))

answer = []
for x in ns:
    x ^= x >> 32
    x ^= x >> 16
    x ^= x >> 8
    x ^= x >> 4
    x ^= x >> 2
    x ^= x >> 1
    answer.append("odd" if x & 1 else "even")
print(*answer)
